Let me tell you who does what on this team, because people always ask. Bruno opens the dashboard at seven, before anybody else arrives, and he reads the overnight numbers first. He does not decide anything on his own. He tells the rest of us what moved, and that is his job. Everything above ten thousand goes to a human, and the model handles the rest by itself. Paula reviews those cases, one by one, and she writes a line about each of them. And there is one thing I do not allow on this team. Nobody changes a limit without a written reason. Nobody. Three months later nobody remembers why the limit moved, and then we cannot explain the number to anybody who asks.

People ask me if a model is smart. That is the wrong question. A model is very good at one thing only: it repeats the same decision a million times without getting tired and without changing its mind. That is worth a lot of money, and it is also the danger. The model never asks whether the rule behind it is still the right rule. It cannot ask that. It only knows the world it learned from, and the world moves. So when the rule goes wrong, and one day it does, the model does not answer for it. The engineer who built it does not answer for it either. The person who wrote the policy answers for it, and that person has to read the numbers every week to know when the rule stopped working.
